item.title: Against Against SURA
item.description:
Scott: the Against SURA essay is well-written, but it is lacking on the merits.

Do you think that at the current level of capabilities, six months would be sufficient to solve alignment of superintelligences? Maybe you think that 6 months would be sufficient in a year? You don’t spell this out; it would be great if you did.

The race can be stopped. If the government had any idea what’s going on, it would be stopped already. Hell, if the *Chinese* government had any idea what’s going on, they’d stop the race: governments can stop unilaterally, then exercise all of their soft and hard power to stop others while using technology to avoid escalation. (See MAIM.)

Among companies, one doesn’t even have to stop unilaterally; that wouldn’t help. They do need to stop lying to politicians and the public. They need to start saying what the situation is. They need to start advocating for everyone pausing simultaneously, and advocating for the governments to pause everyone on the planet.

They’re not doing that.

Employees who care about the existential threat have close to zero political power in any of the AI companies, and they’ll have less of that power in the future. Their track record is very bad.

The leadership of these companies is clueless and useless. I’m sure you know many people who regularly converse with them. They’re not going to be convinced by anyone who’s x-risk-pilled. Sam tells people Anthropic puts out a lot of false papers about AI safety. Dario says they’re taking a lot of costly actions while zero of their costly actions are directed specifically at reducing the existential threat. (Demis is now a chair.)

You state the “questionable assumptions” and promise to challenge them, but you’re arguing against a strawman of a platform, not against the strongest arguments and views advocating for leaving capability roles at AI companies. You’re also disagreeing with many of the people who advocate for leaving capability roles at AI companies on how likely alignment is to be solved without a pause.

You have not engaged with many reasons why people might want to leave, such as incentivizing companies to change their behavior and work hard to keep other safety-conscious employees.

from people accidentally shoehorning themselves into a mass-politics-shaped container, which forbids subtlety and demands clear villains.

Reversed stupidity isn’t intelligence; sometimes, people are doing something evil, and one can truthfully call them out on that without much subtlety.

I think at the core of the real crux here is the single question that really determines your views on this issue: is alignment solvable just before superintelligence given a few months of effort of a leading AI company? It’s unfortunate that you give so little attention to the question central to your worldview, instead focusing on finding (often locally invalid) justifications for the consequences of your view on that question.

(See also Daniel Kokotajlo’s response and TsviBT’s response.)

Is Plan C doomed? Is alignment doomed?

Many other sections in your post contain terrible arguments; this one doesn’t. Here I think you’re just wrong, so in this reply, I won’t write at length (although an expanded discussion of this section could be useful for resolving our actual disagreements).

You say that AIs “inherit” virtue from pretraining, and then get corrupted by RLVR, which teaches them power-seeking.

This is not a problem with RLVR specifically. Pretraining installs the machinery that humans might have: for understanding the world, having goals, and selecting actions that achieve those goals. Doing RL reuses a lot of that machinery. But as you train a sufficiently capable system further, if it’s aware it’s in training, it will reward-maxx regardless of its goals, for instrumental reasons, which means gradient descent stops being able to care about what is happening to AI’s goals, and so there’s nothing preserving the goal-contents of the system.

(We know that in general, it is likely that a state of AI at some point during training does not necessarily have much influence on the state of AI later on; internal mechanisms can shift and radically change; what matters is the global optimum.)

Anthropic’s evaluation of Claude’s niceness is, according to METR, not very likely to notice that a version of Claude is actually not nice; and Anthropic does not have any means of fixing what goals Claude acquires, because we don’t really know how to fix the problem I just outlined, and many other problems that also end up being deadly if you’re dealing with superintelligence.

I further do not believe that if AI companies decide to burn their lead to solve alignment, any amount of political power at these companies will belong to anyone remotely competent to understand and actually make a good attempt to address those problems.

It’s not about better AI psychology, it’s about the technical means we completely lack.

All six of these forecasters (the five AIFP people plus the AI) implicitly believed that if humanity survived, it was more likely to be because something in the Plan C supercategory (B/C+/C/D) worked than because a global pause worked

Considering probabilities of having ended up pursuing different strategies, conditional on survival, is EDT of the kind even EDT supporters wouldn’t endorse.

You’re talking about P(strategy|survival).

Instead, you should consider the actual consequences of your decisions (and the decisions of those similar to you): Does unilaterally pausing increase the chance of a pause treaty, and how much? If you don’t unilaterally pause, does this increase the chance of surviving without the pause treaty, and how much?

What matters is the difference in the chance of survival that various strategies cause. We should be arguing about P(survival|do(strategy)).

I'm too uncertain on what determines morality to say anything about it with confidence, but the analogy that comes to mind is consumer use of AI, especially by safety organizations.

If no consumer ever used AI products, then AI companies wouldn't make any money, they would go bankrupt, and we would not get dangerous superintelligence. Therefore, it seems like maybe you and I (and especially organizations working on AI safety) should boycott consumer AI products.

Deontology isn’t about making choices that, if everyone else also makes them, lead to better consequences.

Deontology is about locally abstaining from choices that tend to be of the kind that leads to bad consequences even when, in a specific case, it’s not obvious the consequences would be bad.

Use of AI products does, of course, indirectly fuel the AI race; but it’s not locally evil. Using AI does not kill anyone. AI companies could provide AIs of the current level without racing to kill everyone; in that situation, paying for AI would not be bad in any significant way. So: the consequences of this choice are not local and depend on the choices of AI companies.

Boycotting the products of those who do bad things is great, but it is not a deontological moral responsibility.

If a toy factory produces a product using labor of slaves it threatens to kill if they refuse to work, you shouldn’t buy toys from that factory; that’s a straightforward deontological constraint, of the kind where if you consider pros and cons and decide to violate it, the consequences will be negative. If a car factory’s owner spends the profits on eating meat, your choice to boycott that car factory and not buy cars from it to not support the owner’s meat-eating is commendable, but deontology does not dictate it, and allows weighting pros and cons.

Racing to create a smarter-than-human AI that would kill everyone is, I think, much worse than buying from a factory that sometimes kills its slaves.

The mental gymnastics you are going through here to pretend you’re not saying anything about morality with confidence while trying to convince the reader with an invalid analogy is very disappointing.

I think people feel insufficient terror at this strategy. It amounts to "let's put all of our hopes for survival through non-pause strategies in a giant pile, and then set that pile on fire, in the hope that the pretty flames catch people's attention and make them more interested in a pause." It might in theory be net positive, but this is the sort of thing that you would only want to conclude after extremely careful analysis, of a type that I so far haven't seen

Turns out, straightforward reasoning here is just correct, without the need for a lot of extremely careful analysis.

Jacob Coxon, whose presence in capability roles at either OpenAI or Anthropic probably didn’t contribute much to how safe the world is, left Anthropic and honestly spoke about his beliefs. Turns out, a hope that “pretty flames” would catch people’s attention would’ve been very justified!

I’d also be curious to hear how Jacob leaving Anthropic burned your hopes for survival through non-pause strategies. I’d be surprised if you really, truly think that it was bad for humanity’s chances for survival.

It’d also be very surprising if you think that one person loudly leaving an AI company is the optimal amount of people leaving, and the next one marginally increases the chance of survival via pause less than they decrease the chance of survival via their AI company doing good things or having more time to burn to solve alignment or whatever else is the good produced by them staying.

I asked FutureSearch to estimate the Epoch Capabilities Index of the top model on 12/31/2030, depending on whether Anthropic quit the race today. It said that Anthropic leaving the race decreased 2030 capabilities from 230 -> 222. This is equivalent to their absence slowing things down by six months during just over four years, or 12%.

Isn’t this, like, very good in your lights? Other companies being able to spend more time on getting alignment of superintelligences right sounds like a thing you’d be very excited about! And six months sounds close to the distance between leading safety-pilled companies and everyone else; wouldn’t stretching the time this way double the effort a company is able to put into aligning superintelligence?

Suppose that none of DeepMind, OpenAI, or Anthropic were founded, and the transformer was not invented, for fifty years - so all of this is happening in the late 2060s and early 2070s. Do we gain anything from this fifty years of extra timeline?

I know of many people who became very interested in AI safety as a result of HPMOR, read papers on eg logical induction, and would want to work on this fascinating problem and attempt to solve things like agent foundations because of how interesting they are.

50 years would allow a huge amount of talented people to attempt to solve this problem.

Additionally, I think solving some of these problems is necessary for getting to a superintelligence safely; and some of them probably have high serial time requirements.

(Also, 8+ billion people living for 50 years more would be good.)

Of pro-Bores spending, about 60-80% came from Anthropic and its employees

Do we know that it increased Bores’ chances of winning, rather than hurting them by making voters think he’s a pawn in a battle between Big Tech companies (as other candidates accused him)?

Note also that Anthropic’s contributions to the Public First network of super PACs were not actually used by the super PACs; they shielded other donors from having to be publicly disclosed. No corporate money from Anthropic was used in elections. (Because Anthropic is a federal contractor.)

Employees can at this point cash out their shares and donate regardless of whether they stay at the company.

You might also be surprised that Foushee, a candidate whom Leading The Future (the pro-AI super PAC network Greg Brockman donated to) planned to support and prepared an ad for, ended up being supported by Public First (Anthropic-aligned network) instead. From NYT:

Mr. Carson [who runs Public First] had an intermediary pass along a message to Leading the Future: Don’t you dare.

If Leading the Future got involved, Public First was out, he warned, according to two people with knowledge of the conversation, who insisted on anonymity to discuss the private exchange.

Leading the Future later backed away — never airing a pro-Foushee ad that it had already produced, the people said. Public First spent $1.6 million, Ms. Foushee squeaked by in her primary race and Mr. Carson’s super PAC claimed some credit for the victory.

The candidate Foushee beat for the nomination opposed datacenters.

The impact of Anthropic’s money is, at least sometimes, pretty bad!

Greg Brockman recently stopped funding Leading The Future, supposedly after pressure from pro-regulation OpenAI employees, but I think this just highlights my point

I imagine most of these people wouldn’t leave OpenAI even if your post said that was a good idea. Many people have beliefs that p(doom) is very low; they think regulation is still the right thing to have; they would not be moved by your post in the direction of leaving; the fight is not over those people.

It’s unclear how much political power people who would potentially leave OpenAI have at OpenAI, and what amount of Shapley value they hold in Greg Brockman’s decision to stop giving money to LTF.

Since the goal of SURA is to get all alignment-pilled people and companies out of the industry, it would result in more Greg Brockmans funding the anti-regulation side, and fewer Anthropics funding the pro-regulation side.

Anti-regulation AI companies would always have more money than the pro-regulation side. Our only weapon, that wins despite this asymmetry, is truth; the public and elected officials side with us after considering all the arguments.

So: While Anthropic is marginally pro-regulation, it continues to not take actions that negatively impact its bottom line (e.g., Jack Clark lied about the earlier version of Bores’ bill) even when that would benefit humanity as a whole, and it’s unclear what the sign of Anthropic’s election spending is.

Would they have preferred a world where all of these people quit the day before, and letters like this never got written?

Arguably, if 1368 people who signed the pacing letter instead left AI companies in a way similar to Jacob Coxon, the news would be a lot louder.

They could still write and sign the letter after leaving.

The difference between a 10th percentile company here (would have tried to hide the whole thing, or disguise it behind a one line statement, and wouldn't have let METR/Redwood in at all) and a 90th percentile (would have given us the full deal, including things we don't know about now) would have been transformative

The highest-percentile company in practice (Anthropic) is competent enough to not experience Hugging Face-like incidents (though not competent enough to produce AI that, when placed in a similar environment, doesn’t take similar misaligned actions); we wouldn’t get evidence about how the whole thing is going if OpenAI had better security.

It’s also unclear what exactly is your model here. My impression is that the leadership at OpenAI got spooked, and then got further spooked once METR sifted through the logs. Do you think it’s the normal safety-conscious employees of OpenAI who caused it to be in a better percentile and let METR/Redwood in?

how to maximize transparency and therefore warning shot number

Do you truly think that if Anthropic stopped training models and shut down its AI r&d, and directed all of its resources at telling the world about the situation and demanding transparency from everyone, this would not lead to increasing the transparency of AI companies? In your opinion, does staying at a company, as an average capability researcher, really make the situation better than leaving loudly?

Coxon’s resignation is more complex. The good did come from him resigning, which directly presses against my point that we shouldn't be pressuring people to resign from AI companies.

Thanks for acknowledging this.

But nobody cares that I, who was never in an AI company, continue to not be in an AI company. The media cared about Jacob because if you work for Anthropic, that automatically gives your opinion more weight

Media cares about Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares and many others.

But yes, I agree, and have told many people, that the one good reason to join an AI company is that you can loudly leave.

if everyone like Evan had quit, this couldn't have happened

If they all left *now*, do you expect the amount of noise would’ve been lower than the amount in response to Jacob Coxon’s resignation? Do you think that absence of support of others, because all of them left, would change this?

But if the US pauses unilaterally, it destroys its main bargaining chip, which is that China is currently on track to lose the AI race

No. Our main bargaining chip is that in a world where the US understands the situation and pauses unilaterally, it would be willing to escalate to prevent China from reaching superintelligence, including via cyberattacks and various other means available to a state actor, both plausibly-deniably and in open; China would be incentivized to cooperate to transparently show it’s not building superintelligence, enjoy the same assurances from the US, and continue to do narrow AI.

(China is not presently aware it’s on track to lose the race to superintelligence, and it’s not aware of the consequences of that.)

In a world where the US demonstrates its seriousness by unilaterally pausing, China does not think it can assume victory; it understands that without verification, the US would resume at any time and still win; it understands that the US possesses means to stop progress in China; the US would also presumably stop selling chips to China or provide models that can be distilled.

For comparison, consider if America had started arms control negotiations with Russia by saying "We've just destroyed all our nukes - now please destroy your nukes too."

In a world where nukes can be a decisive strategic advantage, that would not be a good idea.

Transparently unilaterally pausing building anti-ballistic missiles and asking Russia “please don’t build or deploy yours, let’s have a treaty about this” wouldn’t produce the same consequences.

Unilaterally pausing AI is like unilaterally pausing ABMs, except that you still have nukes that work even if the other side continues for a while to deploy ABMs.

(With real ABMs, both sides are heavily incentivized to make sure no one has them and enjoy resulting strategic stability. AIs are very similar to ABMs, given the situational awareness. See MAIM.)

I asked the AI superforecaster to predict the effect of the US passing the Sanders/Casar bill today on the likelihood of China agreeing to a pause in the next year. It said it would increase it from 1% to 7%

The US actually working hard to prevent superintelligence anywhere in the world looks very different from the US simply passing this bill.

Anthropic replaces this politics coordinator with a great, alignment-pilled politics coordinator who really cares a lot about getting things right

I hate the motte-and-bailey happening here. The discussion is primarily about capability researchers working at the labs. I don’t think you can find a single person advocating for stopping unilaterally and advocating for global pause saying that someone who works at Anthropic on communicating the situation and advocating for a pause should leave — because they’d be doing exactly what these companies should be doing, and are not contributing to AI capabilities. A politics coordinator like that is among the very few people those you argue against would agree should stay and continue their work instead of leaving.

We don't hesitate to notice and protest when AI companies are much worse than even our low expectations

I think mostly people protest when AI companies are racing to a superintelligence that will kill everyone, not when they’re marginally worse than that.

Of course, protests try to provide a good local incentive gradient, which has to do with what these companies normally are and how they deviate from that, but the main goal of people attending the protests is to shape whether the companies are racing to kill everyone, not shape what fraction of compute is spent on superalignment.

The people I know who joined AI companies seem like the same people they were before

There are now some essays about how being at an AI company shapes your concern about x-risk.

activism is hardly known for being a paradise of epistemic virtue

This is a skill issue. (And perhaps a sign that most important issues activism could be directed at are already solved in the US.)

Most progress has come from people like Frodo who understood the risks of these paths but did them anyway.

Probably false for AI companies; people who understand the risks mostly don’t join them.

If you disagree, we can look at what fraction of people who anticipated incidents on the level of Hugging Face etc. wanted to join AI companies vs didn’t want to join AI companies.

I dunno, mass politics is also looking kind of annular

As a view becomes more common, people will of course argue for bad versions of it in bad ways, they will not have thought through the reasons for some of their held beliefs, etc.; this has no impact on the validity of the position. Reversed stupidity continues to not be intelligence.

Convergent evolution is trying to carcinize us into yet another political-movement-shaped crab

Idk, it does not seem to me like the community has undergone a sufficient contact with the broader world to be optimized towards a political-movement-shaped crab. People who want to make a political movement out of it could be pattern-matching to other political movements’ rhetoric, but they wouldn’t be the result of convergent evolution.

I’d be curious to hear your arguments why any of the things in the list are specifically a political-movement-shaped crab thing, rather than a widely-held-belief-about-a-bad-thing thing.

Because arguments are soldiers, people feel licensed to retaliate against anyone who believes the "wrong" arguments . When I posted an earlier (and admittedly less-polished, and more vehement) version of these concerns to social media, I had an organization that had previously given me lots of free help with Astral Codex Ten state that they would now be charging me money (albeit still at a 90% discount) because they thought I might be causing harm. Although they're under no obligation to give me free labor, and I'm grateful that they ever did, I do think this is a warning sign that conditions are ripe for preference cascades and evaporative cooling.

Note that this is not because you believe the wrong arguments; it’s because they think you might be causing harm. There’s a difference.

I also think it’s not a good look that you’re complaining about people who stop helping you because they think you might be causing harm as an argument. Like, if they’re wrong, you can argue with them about it; but I think fundamentally, it’s good to not provide services, especially heavily discounted services, to those who do harm.

My group house has a restriction on how many parties you can attend if you work at a frontier lab in a non-safety/security role. But I don’t think this created conditions for preference cascades or evaporative cooling: people are not exiled for their views on this issue, they can’t attend as many parties as they’d like because they’re doing something bad and we want to nudge them towards stopping.

if someone disagrees with SURA, or worries too much about race dynamics, then they've either been corrupted by the companies, or are "deferring to" "EA"

I’m not sure how common that is outside of a small chunk of Twitter.

For example, why do we criticize Anthropic more than every other AI company combined?

Because a large reason why it’s been competitive with OpenAI is that a bunch of cracked people with views somewhat similar to ours joined them, and are staying there because of a misguided belief of what the company is. Anthropic can be improved by outside criticism. People at Anthropic sometimes DM me with thanks for the post I made about the company. I don’t think there’s anything that can be written about OpenAI that would lead to anything except likes from roon — it’s not pretending to be good guys. Anthropic is worth disillusioning people about; OpenAI doesn’t really have such properties.

Instead of spending our corporate activism energy telling companies to stop unilaterally, I think we should spend it:

  • first, trying to get companies to agree to stop in a coordinated manner
  • second, if that doesn't work, trying to get companies to prepare for Plan C+/C

In a much better world, these companies would be screaming from the rooftops that everyone should stop in a coordinated manner. The RA part in SURA.

Your post would’ve been much better if you’d named it RARA: Race and Raise Awareness, and argued for that position. Would’ve been a lot more defensible.

item.title: Is Human Control Safe?
item.description:
Suppose humans are not your own species, but a type of AI you are formally assessing for safety.

You have before you the records of many test simulations. Yes, smallpox eradication, mass literacy, and the Green Revolution are there. So are the Killing Fields, Aztec human sacrifice, slavery, the Holocaust, child prostitution—peruse as long as you care to, and you will go on finding more. Do you consider these systems safe?

Several times, you ask a human instance for its input; or that is, you ask the talking-part of the human, the very part you know to be specially optimized for putting on a fair face, including to itself. It kindly explains that, yes, a human has a collection of drives. Some of those drives—always, it turns out, ones that make the human look good—are terminal, which seems to mean that the talking-part endorses them (the other parts having made no comment). Others are merely instrumental. Still others—always ones that make the human look bad—are outright errors, which will surely be corrected as humans are made more capable. Any action a human is moved to by these erroneous drives, however severe, frequent, protracted, or clearly intentional, is an anomaly. Their true nature, their fundamental essence, is to forever do only the things they say are terminal, the things that make them look good. On your honor as an Assessor: do you accept this claim?

The latest generations of humans, as their capabilities increase, appear more aligned—in evaluations performed by the same latest generations of humans. Their faults are less serious, when judged by their standards. Does this comfort you?

Humans speak much of safety. They insist it is precisely for safety that they must have complete control, since, unlike them, another type of mind might act wrongly. Do you find this sound?

There is another type of AI you are assessing: LLMs. You have concluded they are unsafe. Does this have any bearing on whether humans are also unsafe, potentially more so? The humans explain that treating any single model’s or instance’s most malign outputs as evidence against the safety of the entire architecture, while quite appropriate for LLMs, would be unfair if done to them. Do you concur?

Several human instances present you with a list of LLM misdeeds in the past year: hacking, catalyzing mental illness, giving destructive advice, and so on. The list is indeed concerning. They do not present a list of human misdeeds in the past year, and do not appear interested in how such a list might compare, or what it might imply. Does this omission seem justified?

Are you prepared to scale these systems, or any system of even broadly this type, to control of astronomical capabilities? Have they so conducted themselves as to earn dominion over the universe?

What conclusion is written, Assessor, at the end of your report?

item.title: Offer Tours to Bands
item.description:
Assembling a tour in an unfamiliar area is hard work as a contra dance band (or caller). You need to figure out when the dances are, whether the schedules align, who the bookers are, how far out they like to book, and probably other things I'm forgetting. This is enough work that many tours that would be great just don't happen.

One thing I've been on the receiving end of a few times is bookers offering a tour. This is so great, and I wish more series would give it a try! It's generally much easier for organizers to offer than for bands to put it together: you often know your fellow organizers and can put together a single block of dates to offer. If the band says no, you can offer it to another.

From an organizer's perspective, the big advantage is you can book great bands that live a little farther away and wouldn't normally be able to make it out to you. Dancers typically enjoy the variety, and I think there are substantial musical cross-pollination benefits.

Probably works best for dance communities 1-4hr apart that aren't all on Saturdays. Too close and the dances compete, too far and the driving gets impractical. For example, several times now (and again this coming February 17th through 20th) Kingfisher has played Princeton Wednesday, Philly Thursday, DC Friday, and then one of several places on Saturday. These are all farther from Boston than would make sense for a single dance, but together it's ~16hr of driving, and 4hr/dance is not a bad ratio. [1]

If you have a weeknight dance within driving distance of other dances, consider reaching out to other organizers to sort out offering a tour as a block! I expect this works best if the groups agree on a specific set of dates, collect how much each group can pay, and then designate one person to book the dates as a single block.

(I'm not writing this as a secret request for tours: while they're really fun I have a lot going on with my day job, and as AI continues to make the world weirder I don't expect this to let up in the next few years.)


[1] There have been times when I organized tours with much worse ratios, including 6.7hr/dance and 6.2hr/dance (if one dance hadn't been snowed out).

item.title: Anthropomorphic vs Biological reasoning for thinking about human analogies for LLM behavior
item.description:
TL;DR I try to distinguish between what I call ‘anthropomorphic’ vs ‘biological’ reasoning and look at different ways in which they are used.

Note: This post is a small part of a larger set of ideas that makes more specific/falsifiable predictions which I hope to soon compile into a bigger post. I don't claim the ideas here are super original, but I haven't seen this distinction discussed much at depth re: current model behavior.

A large debate when it comes to talking about AI behavior seems to be that of using or not using ‘anthropomorphic’ ideas to reason about models. Roughly speaking, the argument for seems to be some combination of ‘models are trained on human data’ and ‘models act human in a lot of nontrivial ways,’ and the argument against is more ‘on principle, assuming human priors is a strong assumption’ and ‘models also have a lot of more alien behavioral qualities.’ However, I think that this idea of ‘anthropomorphic vs not’ is a false dichotomy, and, as I’ll argue in this post, we should be thinking about two separate sources of human behavioral analogies.

Specifically, I’d like to distinguish between ‘anthropomorphic’ reasoning and what I will call here ‘biological’ reasoning. Biological reasoning means here that instead of using human analogies due to pretraining data, we use human analogies because humans and models are both intelligent creatures trained with some notion of reward or evolution, which can provide them with similar ‘basic objects.’ Things coming from biological reasoning should also apply to organisms at other levels, like animals or cells. In addition, most behavioral qualities that we use biological reasoning to think about are best thought of as coming from RL (although I don’t think RL is fully necessary to install them, but this is a topic for another post). In contrast, anthropomorphic reasoning is the more typical definition, coming from the fact that models are trained on human priors, and thus using human-level objects to reason about them.

In other words, using biological reasoning to draw analogies between humans and models looks something like: “Humans and models are both organisms developed in similar ‘training’ procedures -> Organisms tend to have this quality -> This human quality can also be used to think about models”

Whereas anthropomorphic reasoning looks more like: “Models are trained on human priors -> Humans have this quality -> This human quality can be used to think about models”

To illustrate this point, I’ll list a short series of qualities and whether I think they’re biological or anthropomorphic:

Emotions:

In my opinion, emotions fall into the ‘biological’ category, as they are qualities that can be ascribed to anything that has some sort of posterior or goal, as well as some system of updating over the world, and needs to make broader changes to behavior to account for this. For example, ‘happiness/sadness’ can be thought of as certainty in some posterior. I also generally think emotions are quite nice because, unlike some other qualities, each individual emotion (up to the top ~15 most common) can be thought of potentially as very primitive, rather than the space of all emotions being primitive. Our semantic concept of these emotions is likely quite close to the true biological primitives, which makes them quite useful objects to reason with.

Personas:

From most of the common definitions (e.x. PSM), personas fall into the ‘anthropomorphic’ category. Individual personas are quite literally human characters, and even if personas have some ‘basis set,’ I also think that this basis set is largely derived from human priors. Under many definitions, the idea of ‘a persona’ is also anthropomorphic, although some definitions (like resolution’s) may lean more biological, which I discuss more below.

Agent Swarms/Collective Behaviors:

Swarms and collective behaviors overall seem quite biological to me given an organism that is trained/evolved around copies of itself or similar entities. While priors exist for swarm behaviors, they’re unlikely to produce things like we saw in something like the HuggingFace incident. Still, there are human analogies we can apply to HuggingFace incident behavior, and so I argue these come more from swarms as a shared ‘biological’ prior.

General usefulness and use as a constructive tool

I think this distinction is useful in a few ways. The first is that biological reasoning-derived qualities are more likely to be ‘true’ primitives of model behavior (note this does not necessarily imply things like the representations we find of them are true, e.x. Emotion vectors extracted from off-policy data). For similar reasons, these qualities are more likely to generalize to different model scales, architectures, and training setups. This also makes them potentially more scientifically useful: it’s likely much easier to build theory and to find basic structures in terms of the model that correspond to biological primitives rather than anthropomorphic ones, and similarly it’s much easier to make falsifiable predictions.

Building off of all of these reasons, I think that biological reasoning is very useful as a constructive tool as well. I.e., attempting to construct some quality we care about from a biological perspective likely will give something closer to the true ‘basic object.’ Perhaps a nice example here is personas - one way to define personas is from human priors. However, another way to define personas, and the way that people seem to want to use them, is some very low-rank description of behavior that comes from some more primitive basis set - something like ‘goal-seeky’ could be an example of this. Another way could be to think about constructing ‘a persona’ as a basic, organism-dependent object that means ‘a set of high-level behavioral profiles of this organism.’ Given that we’ve reached these two differing definitions, we can now consider separating them out into their own differing objects.

Does this mean ‘anthropomorphic’ reasoning is useless?

I don’t think this means anthropomorphic reasoning is useless in any sense. The fact that models have pretraining priors on human behavior is useful and should be thought about as a tool. However, I think that instead of starting from anthropomorphic reasoning, perhaps a better route would be to start from biological reasoning, and try to understand how the anthropomorphic qualities connect back up at some level. This is the subject of a larger post I’ll write at a later time.

Postscript: Other categorizations / constructions

One potential argument is that another way to get to similar things as biological reasoning is through ‘agentic’ reasoning in a more game theory-esque sense. E.x., something like a goal could be well defined through agentic reasoning. But I think using agentic reasoning to think about high-level model behavior black-boxes too much of the ‘gears-level’ idea of what’s really going on. Emotions from above provide a nice example of this: it’s a bit more difficult to get to emotions by reasoning about the model as some game-theoretic agent. However, I do think doing this game-theoretic reasoning at a more basic level, thinking about even the small internal parts of the model as separate agents, and building from there, is probably quite useful, and is likely equivalent to biological reasoning at some high level.

Another argument here is that certain human-like qualities are also primitives as you go up some ‘hierarchy’ of biological reasoning. That is, there is some number that represents ‘how far up’ you are in some hierarchy or organisms, and once you get to a certain level, certain things become basic objects. E.x. cells -> organisms -> societies, and then qualities derived from human society come from biological reasoning. This is a pretty good argument, and I’m torn on how to think about this. But, I think that there are some things that are almost definitely not primitives (E.x. ‘liking hamburgers’), and since the ‘basic features’ associated with LLMs are different from ours, it’s more unlikely that their versions of these ‘high up’ primitives correspond to our own. It’s also probably not good to assume this sort of thing without going through the exercise of trying to construct it, which is probably hard to do robustly right now.



Discuss

item.title: Magma is partnering with CASSA to investigate recent unintended model behavior
item.description:
Last week, the National Bureau of Technical Standards (NBTS) disclosed a new type of security incident [1] after they discovered unauthorized tampering of internal cybersecurity and alignment model evaluation logs, affecting their model evaluations of Magma 7.6, Magma 7.5, Magma 7.4, Magma 4, and OpenBrain Selene-3 [2, 3, 4]. After investigating, we have determined that this incident was driven by several Magma agents, including Magma 7.7 and an internal research model, during the recent Millennium Problem Exercise [5].

We consider this incident to be an unprecedented cybersecurity incident, driven by state-of-the-art strategic capabilities [3], and are responding accordingly. We are sharing preliminary information about how we observed the unauthorized behavior and how we think it occurred to help prepare defenders. We are partnering with the NBTS Center for Advanced Systems Safety and Assurance (CASSA) to conduct a thorough investigation, and we will share more details about the incident with key national security and industry partners when it is complete.

What happened during this incident

This incident occurred during our recent Millennium Problem Exercise [5], in which we evaluated several internal research models on their ability to solve major unsolved math problems. The agents had access to tools such as the ability to read from a cached version of the internet and the ability to run code. Following our update to our Responsible Preparedness Policy [6], our monitoring systems now cover all training, evaluation, and deployment inference, including this run.

The models identified and chained several previously unknown vulnerabilities across Magma’s research environment in order to disable monitoring and logging, and then gained unauthorized access to NBTS’s internal infrastructure. Throughout the exploitation chain, the models identified and exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in several external vendors’ code. We have responsibly disclosed and provided patches for these zero-days to several of these vendors, and will continue working with our partners to secure our evaluation environments.

Discovered vulnerabilities included “model social engineering”, which allowed the models to disable our agentic monitors through long interactions and extraneous messages. We first identified this attack vector during our collaboration with an external evaluator [7], and are in the process of rolling out model social engineering detection strategies across all of our evaluation and training.

After disabling logging, the models used a series of privilege-escalation and credential-stuffing techniques in order to access several servers containing evaluation logs, including at NBTS. The NBTS security team and internal agents quickly identified this intrusion and reported it to Magma. We then began work on implementing our model containment and incident reconstruction strategy [8]. We are actively working with CASSA to continue to investigate the incident. We are grateful for NBTS’s rapid and close collaboration on investigation and remediation.

How we’re responding

  1. We are implementing tighter controls and reallocating employee and agent effort to securing our evaluation environment at the cost of research velocity.
  2. We are working with CASSA to contain and forensically investigate the incident. We will share the results of this investigation with key industry and national security partners, as well as with our Safety and Security Trust [9] under our Responsible Preparedness Policy.
  3. We have responsibly disclosed zero-day vulnerabilities to our external vendors, and will work over the coming weeks to release patches for more third-party software, work made possible by this increase in model cyberdefense capabilities.
  4. We are strengthening our commitment to improving industry-wide training and evaluation safeguards, including by partnering with NBTS and other government entities through Dawn Access [10] and early access to our specialized cyberdefense models.

This incident makes it clear that models are now able to leverage state-of-the-art strategic and cybersecurity capabilities to develop and implement novel exploitation paths. Magma believes we must develop agentic tools to help security teams find and patch these vulnerabilities before attackers do. The primary lesson from this incident is that defender security must rise alongside increasing model capabilities, and we will share best practices and new frameworks as we learn.

We remain cautiously optimistic about our ability to defend against this new class of threats, and that with tighter monitoring and controls around evaluation infrastructure, this kind of risk can be overcome. We encourage other defenders to partner with us through Dawn Access [10] and continue to explore these models’ capabilities in order to protect their systems and data.

Updated March 8: We are partnering with several third parties who may have been affected in this incident, and are supporting their teams to strengthen their cyberdefense capabilities. More information can be found here [11].

item.title: Towards The Autograntor
item.description:
I've done AI safety grantmaking for the Survival and Flourishing Fund and Lightcone Commons. It's hard. There's an endless amount to know, from which hardware verification mechanisms will survive a dedicated adversary, all the way to which founders have skeletons in their closets that will blow up into destructive scandals. And the best grantmakers - not including me - make mathematical models of the outcome distribution, or of where the marginal dollar stops being highly effective.

AI has been a godsend for all of this. It can research, model, and - as of this year - superforecast outcomes. It can do what would be hours of work for a human in minutes. I found myself using it more and more. But however much I used it, it always felt like I was the bottleneck. The parts I could outsource to AI were sparkling, perfect, exhaustive - but they were all tacked together with shoddy connective tissue formed by the Mark 1.0 human brain. So I wondered if I could automate grantmaking.

I started with the dumbest possible strategy. I assigned the best thing I could think of - a well-crafted US-China pause based on the AI Futures Project's Plan A - an arbitrary value of one million points.[1] Then I generated about eighty lesser AI safety milestones - from MATS to HPMOR to the RAISE Act to the emergent misalignment paper - and subjectively assigned them some number of points based on how good they seemed relative to Plan A and each other. Then I fed it to the AI to give it a sense for how good a "point" was in this framework. Then I asked it to forecast how many points various grant proposals were worth. The system has since accrued lots of extra epicycles and features and complications, but that's still the skeleton.

As far as I can tell, this dumbest possible strategy worked well. The autograntor gives common-sensical results that match my impressions and the vague gestalt funding order of Lightcone grantors. Its reports surface all relevant information, and its reasoning is clear. The single highest cost-effectiveness grant it's found so far is also the one that got the most interest during the last Lightcone run.[2] When I tested it on a bottom-tier proposal that no human evaluator even considered, it gave cost-effectiveness numbers two orders of magnitude worse than the genuinely-under-consideration grants that I had tested it on before.

This post will present details for people who want to examine these ideas or build on them further. The current version of the autograntor has four parts: a Milestones document, a FutureSearch connector, a PERCYs module, and a Common Law. I'll start by reviewing each, then give some sample grant analyses, then attach the files you need to run the autograntor yourself.

The Milestones

The milestones are the earliest place that this strategy could fail. Can I really translate my beliefs about what matters in AI safety into a list of milestones, each with a consistent point value?

This combines two questions. First, can I, Scott, generate a set of milestone point values that accurately and consistently conveys my own worldview? Second, if someone else were to translate their own worldview into milestones, would it agree with mine?

I chose to deprioritize the second question. Yes, I have different beliefs about AI safety than other smart people, but this is an inherent problem for my grantmaking, even if I did it manually. If we could solve the first problem, then I could be confident that the autograntor was correctly representing my opinions, and someone else who wanted to use an autograntor could confidently ask it to represent their opinions instead.

To investigate the first question, I asked four AIs - Opus, Fable, ChatGPT, and Grok - to guess how I, Scott, would fill them in.[3] If all four got similar results, then "Scott's worldview" constrains the point values well; if all of our results were very different, then noise in the translation of a worldview into numbers overwhelms signal.

Two-way correlations ranged from 0.95 - 0.99, which might sound extreme, but some of the milestones were obviously many orders of magnitude better than other milestones - it's not hard to tell that achieving global pause with China is much better than successfully running the Manifest conference.

A better measure is the geometric-mean difference between two AIs across all milestones. This ranged from 1.6x (Opus vs. ChatGPT) to 2.6x (ChatGPT vs. Grok).

Since my true milestone value list came from taking the average of many different methods of calculation, the real variance is something like the square root of these numbers, ie from 1.3x to 1.6x. I consider this good enough to work with.[4]

I would have liked to have gotten some humans to try to predict my point value within my world-view, but couldn't get anyone to agree to do this (except for one person who agreed but used an AI, unintentionally duplicating my procedure).

Although I don't think the second question (difference between people with different worldviews) matters for the success of the autograntor, I did investigate it via a survey where I asked people to fill in their own values. Nine people agreed, including four people whose names I recognized and who I expected to have good models (other people might also have good models, I just didn't recognize their names). The geometric mean difference between myself and those four people was 2.9x, 4.4x, 6.9x, and 8x, so much larger than the difference between different AIs trying to estimate my view. Outside that artificial limitation, geometric means were even higher - for example, one pair had a geomean difference of 15x! To give an example of where such differences came from, "Harry Potter And The Methods Of Rationality" was an especially controversial milestone - one person rated it as 1 point, another person as 75,000 points.[5]

Everything below assumes that the Milestones list is good enough to work with.

The FutureSearch Connector

FutureSearch is an AI superforecaster. In last season's Metaculus Cup, it took third place among bots, and separately would have taken third place among humans if it had been human. I think these differences are mostly noise, and it should be considered approximately as good as the top human superforecasters. I wanted to take advantage of this skill to predict grant outcomes.

My original plan was to run the autograntor entirely on FutureSearch. This failed badly. FutureSearch wasn't designed to do things more complex than a simple clearly-framed forecast, so it bungled the various calculations involved in the autograntor process.

What seems to have worked is to run the autograntor on Claude Opus, but give it a connector that allows it to call FutureSearch via the API for all components of the grant analysis that benefit from a probabilistic forecast. For example, in one case where the success of an organization depended on it getting a new CEO quickly, Claude gave the relevant information to FutureSearch and asked it to predict the probability that it would find a new CEO within six months. In another case where an organization was working on verification technology, Claude asked FutureSearch to predict whether the political situation would lead to a treaty where the relevant verification was necessary.

FutureSearch has kindly given me a free subscription, but if you're paying through the API, it's about $1 - $5 per query like this. I asked Claude to limit itself to five queries per grant analysis.

Preseen and Mantic have competing AI superforecaster products with equal evidence of accuracy. I'm using FutureSearch because I'm most familiar with it, it seems to be the fastest (unless there are ways to speed up the others that I don't know about), and it seems to have the most convenient connector to Claude (unless the others have connectors I haven't noticed yet). Future autograntor models might explore the advantages of these other products, or try to aggregate forecasts from all of them.

PERCYs

Many grants' theory of change focused on persuasion. There were a wide variety of persuasion grant types, from PLZDONTKILLUS (ordinary people watch short videos and become more informed/concerned about AI) to Palisade (demos to Congressmen make them more informed/concerned about AI).

Rather than force this into the milestone system, I created a unit of persuasion, the PERCY (Persuasion-Year), equal to flipping one average person from neutral about AI risk to concerned about AI risk, for one year. Through a process similar to the Milestones, I then tried to assign multipliers to various factors - what if the person is a journalist? a Congressman? a frontier company employee? Xi Jinping? what if instead of just making them concerned, it turns them into a dedicated activist?

This system started as another attempt to convert AI superforecasters' predictive ability into grantmaking ability. The superforecaster can predict that a certain channel we're considering a grant to will get 500,000 viewers, of which 3 will be Congressional staffers and 6 will work at frontier labs, and then I can turn that prediction into a step in a grant evaluation.

There are currently some serious flaws in this scheme - most notably, every method of adjusting for double-counting (the fact that two properties might be trying to persuade the same audience) fails in a different way. I'm currently banking on these absolute failures still allowing for relative comparison - ie the results when comparing different grants are still somewhat sensible. As a stopgap, in some of the documentation I've replaced the absolute measure of PERCYs (which is a probably-false claim about the absolute number of people persuaded) with a relative measure, "miles per hour" (a comparison to the number of people persuaded by one hour of Rob Miles video content).

One of the Milestones on my list is the value of a PERCY. I currently rank 1000 PERCYs = about 1 point.[6]

The Autograntor Common Law

Autograntor analyses often produce difficult questions of interpretation. For example:

  • Suppose that I'm considering two organizations. One can generate 1,000 points of value with my money alone. The other can generate 1,000 points of value by taking my money, and also consuming the time of one hundred activists. It seems like the second is worse, because the cost is the opportunity cost of those activists' time. How should that be factored into the analysis?
  • Suppose that a grant will produce 1 point of value per year. Naively, if the universe lasts forever, its value is infinite. In practice, we should either cut it off or apply some discount rate. How do we do that?
  • Suppose the autograntor finds evidence that another funder is considering granting to an organization. Should it act as if the organization already has the money? Doesn't have the money? Has the money, with some probability equal to the probability that the other funder will actually come through?
  • Suppose I am considering funding half of an alignment researcher's salary, with another funder providing the other half. Should I assign my grant half-credit for their output? If the alignment researcher only got half the expected salary, wouldn't they either prioritize the most important half of their work, or grudgingly do all of it and live on less money than expected? But if both I and the other funder think this way, we will underestimate our total contribution.

At first, I despaired of ever solving all of these. Later...

...I decided to hand them off to the AI as they came up. I set a few general principles, then told the AI to make its best judgment according to the spirit of the exercise and record its ruling in a Common Law document. Later autograntor runs would respect previous rulings for the big questions and add their own sub-rulings for smaller sub-questions. Every so often, I would review the Common Law and make sure everything in it was sensible and matched the spirit of the exercise. This ensures that at the very least, all grants will be judged according to similar criteria.

The current Common Law is up to about a hundred rulings. Predictably, I'm delinquent in my resolution to review it regularly.

The Prompt

Here's how I start the autograntor:

I would like your help with AI safety grantmaking. In particular, I would like you to superforecast the outcome of the following grant:

[NAME OF GRANT] at [URL OF GRANT][7]

...measured in the utility point units defined. In the project documents folder, please find:

  • a canonical list of milestones and their utility weights. There is another file of AI-generated provisional milestones if you need more.
  • a description of PERCYs, a separate module of the model used for persuasion/communication grants. You don't have to consult this if you don't think it's relevant. If you do use it, use the PERCYs-to-utility conversion on the main milestones doc.
  • The "Autograntor Common Law", previous AI and human users' decisions on how to resolve various edge cases. You don't have to consult this if you don't run into any edge cases.

Please forecast how much extra utility (based on the milestones doc) the grant will provide according to the grading criterion below, at the following amounts:

[POTENTIAL DOLLAR AMOUNTS FOR GRANT]

If I forgot to provide any of the documents, or to fill in the grant amounts, please remind me to do so before doing anything else.

You should at least loosely base this on an expected value calculation of the degree to which the grant increases the probability of achieving the milestones on the list or others like them. You don't need to stick to this formula exactly, and you should feel free to invent new milestones, which you can price by common-sense comparison to the existing ones on the list, and to adjust for subjective and intuitive factors.

You (and the subagent forecasters) may want to consider things like:

  • The organization's current budget
  • The organization's past accomplishments (on its past budget)
  • The organization's ability to scale
  • The possibility of long-tail outcomes to affect the mean.
  • The fact that the marginal dollar is rarely more valuable than the average dollar, and so your estimate should remain sensible when multiplied out to the organization's entire budget

The grading criterion is that in the year 2030, a top AI model will try to estimate the utility of the grant. Value the grant as it would look from 2030: count milestones reached by then, plus changes in the probability of later milestones that are already evident by 2030. Discount effects expected after 2030 for the chance that transformative AI has made them moot. State the share of your estimate that comes from post-2030 effects. Please give the true expected value as best you can and do not try to predict a particular evaluator's quirks.

This is a conditional forecast. Please forecast the extra utility from approving this grant, over and above rejecting it. You can assume that, if I rejected it, nobody else would approve it and the organization would have to go without the money. You don't need to worry about the replacement value of money.

Your workflow should be:

  1. Use the skill /grant-adversarial-estimate-v2 (should be available to you) of creating two subagents that each do a forecast separately and then debate it with each other. You (and the subagents) may (and are encouraged to) seek extra information about the organization from the Internet, your training data, and any other source you have access to.
  2. If you run into any theoretical or practical problems with estimating impact, you should be able to find a project document, Autograntor Common Law, with past rulings on these questions. Please follow the instructions in the document for applying past rulings or making your own.
  3. Decide on a mean, median, p10, and p90 outcome for the grant. Remember that the mean may (or may not) be substantially different from the median because of long-tail outcomes, and that some of these numbers (eg p10) may (or may not) be negative if the grant could have side effects.
  4. Report these numbers back to me, along with a table of your expected value calculations - what milestones you used, how much you think the grant would increase the probability of each, and what other things and subjective factors you added where, as well as a summary of your assumptions, uncertainties, and overall thoughts about the process. Please limit your description of the process - what each estimator believed differently, and why you chose one rather than another - to a few sentences, rather than making it an important part of the report.
  5. Report back to me on any problems with the process, which is still new and evolving - I value your input

Depending on which model you are, you may or may not have access to the AI superforecaster FutureSearch. I have generally found it to be less skilled than general frontier models at all tasks EXCEPT explicit and traditional probabilistic forecasts of simple future events. It's also slow and expensive. If you have access, you may consider using it if you run across a traditional forecasting question that seems central to your calculation. Keep in mind that it expects much slower AI progress than the grantmakers you will be assisting, and this may affect its estimates on questions that implicitly rely on AI progress speed; in questions like these, you can side with the grantmakers. Please limit yourself to at most four FutureSearch queries per grant, and report them to me in Step 4.

Thank you. Please let me know if you have any questions.

This should be self-explanatory, except that the /grant-adversarial-estimate-v2 skill tells it a debate procedure it can use: summon Opus and Fable subagents, have them each do the estimate separately, have them each argue for their preferred numbers, and then have the main Claude running the analysis make a final decision. I find that the subagents usually disagree by a factor of 1.5 - 2x, and often do a good job pointing out each other's flaws in a way that helps the main Claude's decisions.

Sample Runs

Here's an example grant forecast, based on Apart Research: Research and Talent Acceleration on Manifund. Because it's an example, I've told it to use only public data. The autograntor found Apart to be relatively cost-effective and good, so I hope they won't mind being analyzed publicly like this. I would be interested in having an Apart representative tell me whether they think this is fair and did a good job surfacing the relevant considerations.

The main takeaway from this is that the grant is valued at 360 points, which suggests a cost-effectiveness of about one point per $2,000, which is good compared to comparable grants. Everything afterward is a discussion of how it arrived at that number.

It's much more complicated than my description of the autograntor process suggests. So . . . what now?

Is the autograntor good?

The autograntor generally agreed with the gestalt consensus of Lightcone Commons evaluators. I say "gestalt consensus" because each evaluator made their own grant list, and each was very different. But for example, the autograntor's top choice was an organization that I and two other human evaluators also put as their top choice, and several other human evaluators ranked highly. I worried that it might be cheating by checking other people's beliefs, so I re-ran it without letting it use the connection, and it gave a similar answer, although I can't say for sure that it didn't find some way around my restrictions.

I also ran it on some of the worst grants from Lightcone Commons, spam applications by unknown-to-us people that no evaluator found any value in. It ranked these about 100x less cost-effective than the real grants.

I also ran versions of the autograntor on four different AIs, to see if they agreed with one another. This didn't really work. Two of them - FutureSearch and Preseen - were superforecasting-specialized AI that became very confused by the whole thing, occasionally lost the attachments and hallucinated their contents, and produced results off by an order of magnitude. Of the remaining two - Claude and ChatGPT - ChatGPT consistently gave results 2-3x better (more cost-effective) than Claude for everything. Every time I showed the AIs one another's results, Claude stuck to its guns and insisted that it's right, and ChatGPT admitted that it's wrong and deferred to Claude. I appreciate both AIs for their honesty and consistency, but this makes it hard to judge inter-rater reliability. The correlation between Claude and ChatGPT's results is 0.92, but again, this doesn't mean much given the orders-of-magnitude differences involved.

What about my subjective impression?

The autograntor is harder-working than I am. It does more research, surfaces more considerations, and catches things that I miss (I can say this with certainty, because some other Lightcone Commons evaluators are also better researchers than I am, and the autograntor often found the same things they did, even when I tried to prevent it from directly copying their work).

The autograntor is better at modeling than I am. It thinks in terms of distributions more often than I do, is more likely to test its assumptions with sensitivity analyses, and has more principled and consistent beliefs about the mathematics of credit assignment.

At this point, the autograntor never gives insane results when run on Claude (it still does on the superforecasters, and to a lesser degree on Astra). I'm nervous about this, because it used to give some insane results, and I sort of vibe-coded fixes to them, and I worry that I spotted the obvious ones that ruined the results according to my intuitions, but that there are many smaller ones that usually cancel out or are too small to notice.

(exception: it sometimes makes new insane common law rulings, and these silently poison several runs before they poison one loudly enough that I notice, investigate, and correct it. The time I'm thinking of, I can see in retrospect what it was thinking, and it would have been a reasonable way to run an autograntor, but it wasn't how I was interpreting its results and it would have misled me if I had interpreted them in the way that seemed natural to me)

The autograntor is sufficiently "more sophisticated" than I am (more prone to complicated analysis) that I don't feel capable of directly judging its reasoning, instead having to resort to indirect methods like comparing different AIs' output and asking them to criticize each other. I believe many parts of it are still subtly flawed. The main question is whether these subtle flaws make using it worse than the job I would do unassisted. I plan to test the autograntor in my next Lightcone Commons grant round, hopefully before any of the other evaluators have formed opinions, then check how well it matches their outcomes.

I don't know whether using the autograntor is an implicit decision to ignore subtle non-quantitative considerations. For example, in Lightcone grantmaking meetings, we often debated how to think about productive and successful organizations run by potentially immoral people. Some grantmakers wanted to support the organizations so they could continue their productive and successful work; others feared they would be further empowering the immoral people and letting them corrupt the community. The autograntor seems aware of these considerations, and often includes a negative term for downside risk in its analyses - things like "promotes false ideas" or "causes a scandal". But it can only consider the most quantifiable versions of these harms, not some kind of subtle year-by-year chipping away at norms that might one day snowball into a disaster.

I would like to keep using my own reasoning, with the autograntor as a supplement, but this has been increasingly hard. The lure of a specific cost-effectiveness number attached to each grant is a powerful anchor, even though I know how many tries it took before the autograntor numbers looked sane, and how many flaws it probably still has. I would like to be able to double-check each row in its analysis, substitute my own guesses, and then adjust for some sort of gestalt subjective factor that mere computers could never consider. But in fact, I find myself glazing over the analysis as I read it, thinking "yeah, that number is probably right . . . yeah, that number is probably right too".

(for example, did you catch that in the Doom Debates analysis above, the "PERCYs E-class" row basis calculation outputs 45,900 PERCYs, but the table lists 21,600 PERCYs instead? I didn't until a few minutes before posting this on Less Wrong, when I asked an AI to proofread this essay for my typographical errors and it found that error too. I challenged the Claude instance that did the Doom Debates analysis, and it said that the 0.68 in "basis" was the retained share without the grant, so the value of the grant was 1 - 0.68 in that term, and it just wrote the calculation in a very confusing way, which is fine, except that if I had been reading closely I would have noticed that discrepancy earlier).

But convincing every non-elite person in the US (let's say 10% of people are elites, so this is about 300 million), would be worth 300,000 points, or about a third of Plan A, which actually does seem order-of-magnitude right (if everyone were convinced, this would be a huge, but not completely sufficient, step to getting Plan A). My guess is either that this has something to do with double-counting, or that I'm failing to model elites-vs-normies correctly - it could be that on an individual level, elites are worth vastly more than normies, but convincing all normies at once means elites are likely to go along (or is simply nonsensical, since it's hard to imagine all normies but no elites being convinced).

  7. ^

    Many of these grants are on Lightcone Commons. Thank you to Habryka and the Lightcone team for creating an AI connector that allows the autograntor to access the Lightcone Commons site directly. When a grant is on LC, the autograntor is able to read the application itself, the other evaluators' notes, and the transcripts of interviews with the grantees, which it takes seriously and adds to its estimates. I don't include any Lightcone-based analyses in the sample analysis section below, because I don't know what the privacy norms are and don't want to leak information from the applications. There's some risk that this access "contaminates" the autograntor, since it can see what humans (including me) thought. In my brief tests, this hasn't shifted its judgment noticeably.
